n: Like Psalm 74, this lament mourns Jerusalem’s fall, probably to Babylon in 587 BC. Foreign nations have invaded God’s own land, defiled his temple, and left Jerusalem in rubble.
The bodies of God’s faithful were left for birds and wild animals — a terrible disgrace in a culture that honored burial.

f.w: meat unto the fowls of the heaven

n: Blood was poured out like water around Jerusalem, and no one was left to bury the dead.
Israel has become a joke to the surrounding nations.
How long, Lord? Will your jealous anger burn forever? God’s jealousy is his fierce, protective love for his covenant people, which they had betrayed.

f.g: God’s passionate zeal for an exclusive covenant relationship.

n: The people ask God to turn his anger instead on nations that don’t know or call on him. Jeremiah used nearly the same words.

f.w: Pour out thy wrath upon the heathen

n: For those nations have devoured Jacob and ruined his homeland.
Don’t hold our ancestors’ sins against us. Let your compassion come quickly to meet us, for we are crushed.
Help us for the honor of your name; rescue us and cover our sins. Their hope rests on God’s character, not their merit.
Why let the nations sneer, “Where is their God?” Show your justice openly by avenging your servants’ blood.
Let the groans of prisoners reach you; by your great power, keep alive those condemned to die.

f.w: those that are appointed to die

n: Pay back our neighbors seven times over for the insults they hurled at you. Seven symbolizes completeness — full justice.

f.g: Into the fold of their robe, as grain poured into a lap.

n: Then we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will thank you forever and tell your praise to every generation. Lament ends in a promise of praise.
